cim: Artificial Intelligence: the challenge lies in the quality of organizational decisions
cim_eredeti: Artificial Intelligence: the challenge lies in the quality of organizational decisions
szoveg_eredeti:
Executive summary: Artificial Intelligence can increase productivity, but its impact depends on the quality of decisions about where and how to apply it. The article discusses the risks of indiscriminate adoption, the workslop phenomenon, leadership responsibility, and the criteria needed to generate real organizational transformation.

Artificial Intelligence has been occupying more and more space in organizations. New tools, applications, and possibilities are continuously emerging, accompanied by a growing expectation of gains in productivity, efficiency, and innovation.

In this movement, many companies began to encourage their teams to use technology, seeking to speed up activities, automate processes, and expand delivery capacity.

But there is one issue that deserves greater attention: are we making the right decisions about where and how to implement Artificial Intelligence?

In the article published in the Harvard Business Review, AI-Generated “Workslop” Is Destroying Productivity, authors Kate Niederhoffer and collaborators offer an important reflection on the effects of incautious AI adoption in the workplace.

Have you heard the expression ‘workslop‘? Authors use it to describe content produced with artificial intelligence that appears to be well crafted but lacks the consistency or depth needed to effectively solve a problem.

In other words, these are deliveries that seem ready but require review, validation, interpretation, and often reconstruction by those who receive them.

A survey conducted by BetterUp Labs in partnership with the Stanford Social Media Lab, with 1,150 full-time workers in the United States, revealed that about 40% had already received content classified as workslop in the previous month. Participants estimated spending, on average, 1 hour and 56 minutes to handle each occurrence, generating impacts on productivity, trust, and collaboration.

Does this sound familiar? You are challenged to implement AI in your routines, and what initially seemed like time savings can actually shift the effort to another stage of the process: reviewing and readjusting the AI-generated product.

This reflection broadens a discussion I consider fundamental: the adoption of Artificial Intelligence does not, by itself, represent an organizational transformation.

Related article: ISI launches MCP Server to bring trusted data and intelligence into clients’ AI workflows – ISI

There is a tendency to associate the advancement of AI with the number of tools implemented, trained employees, or automated activities. However, using more technology does not necessarily mean generating more value.

A report from MIT NANDA, titled The GenAI Divide: State of AI in Business 2025, presented a very striking result: 95% of the organizations analyzed were not achieving measurable returns on their generative AI investments.

When implementation starts with the tool, rather than understanding organizational challenges, we risk automating isolated activities, accelerating low-impact tasks, and producing an even greater volume of information and deliverables.

I’m not underestimating the gains we can achieve by ending a meeting and having minutes with the main points and action plans discussed, or by making our email inboxes more functional, with spam cleaning and prioritizing appointments.

But if the process in which you used AI continues to require the same effort of validation, interpretation, and review, have we really achieved efficiency?

In some cases, we just speed up the production of something that still needs to be fixed.

The same MIT NANDA report points out that more than 80% of surveyed organizations have explored or tested general-purpose generative AI tools such as ChatGPT and Copilot, and nearly 40% report their implementation. However, these tools mainly improve individual productivity, and not necessarily the organization’s financial performance.

The study also identified an important difference between experimenting and effectively incorporating solutions into processes: among organizations that evaluated specific corporate AI tools, 60% reached the evaluation stage, 20% advanced to pilot projects, and only 5% reached production.

And here we return to the initial question: are we making the right decisions about where and how to implement Artificial Intelligence? Where can its application promote a significant change in the way we work and generate results?

Related article: Making Documents Intelligent: How Metadata Powers Market Discovery – ISI

The Harvard Business Review’s reflection also draws attention to the responsibility of leaders in this process.

When organizations set an indiscriminate guideline for everyone to use AI, without clarifying objectives, quality criteria, and expectations about results, they can end up encouraging superficial adoption of the technology.

Demanding speed and delivery volume, without considering the quality of what is being produced, creates a favorable environment for the emergence of the workslop.

This is where leadership needs to go beyond encouraging the use of tools. It needs to demonstrate how to use them intentionally, set quality standards, and encourage a culture of responsible experimentation.

This means allowing teams to explore possibilities, test applications, and learn from the results, while maintaining clarity about goals and responsibility for deliveries.

AI should be incorporated as a collaborative tool, capable of expanding human skills, not as a shortcut to reduce the effort of thinking, analyzing, and deciding.

Related article: Put ISIs hard-to-source intelligence behind your AI workflows – ISI

Perhaps one of the biggest challenges for organizations right now is developing the ability to properly select where to invest efforts in implementing AI.

This will require careful curation of organizational challenges, to understand which problems really compromise outcomes, where the main bottlenecks lie, and which opportunities offer transformative potential.

Some questions can guide this assessment:

This initial curation allows differentiating initiatives that only facilitate specific activities from those that can effectively modify the organization’s ability to act.

I will bring an example from my field of expertise: Market Intelligence. We can use AI to collect data and summarize information. They are useful applications, but we can go further.

Imagine using technology to integrate different sources of information, identify relationships between indicators, recognize signs of market change, and support the construction of scenarios that contribute to strategic decisions.

Did you see the difference? Using AI to expand our analytical capacity, allowing faster connections and interpretations, but always combined with the experience and knowledge of specialists in the field.

This difference needs to be present in investment and prioritization decisions.

Artificial Intelligence offers extraordinary opportunities, but its potential will not be fully harnessed by speed of adoption alone.

We need to develop organizations capable of identifying relevant problems, properly allocating resources, establishing quality criteria, and preparing people to work collaboratively with technology.

We also need to review how we evaluate productivity, going beyond accounting for automated tasks or time saved. It is necessary to understand what was done with that time, which steps were eliminated, what quality was achieved, and what additional value was generated.

After all, if AI speeds up production but increases the effort of review and correction, perhaps we are just shifting the work, not eliminating inefficiencies. And, most importantly, missing the opportunity to direct our increasingly scarce financial efforts and resources toward projects that truly deliver significant gains.

The transformation brought about by Artificial Intelligence begins long before the choice of a tool.
